newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil mining giant goes on the block.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil mining giant goes on the block.

text.p: Brazil's six year-old privatization program will reach its high point next week at the auction of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), the jewel in the Brazilian public sector crown.

With over two years of planning involved, the April 29 CVRD auction will kick off the biggest state selloff in Latin American history and once completed, should raise at least $5.0 billion for the Brazilian government coffers.

"This is the culmination of two years in which the government has committed itself to the task of transfering to private hands another major provider of goods and services," said Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros, head of the National Development Bank, which is responsible for the privatization program.

"Vale" -- as CVRD is universally refered to -- stands out among Latin American public sector corporations principally because it is profitable, efficient and innovative in the use of mining technologies.
With over 15,400 employees, an annual sales of $5.0 billion and total assets of $10.4 billion, CVRD posted a 1996 profit of $632 million.
Its Carajas mine, deep in the Amazon rain forest, holds enough iron ore to secure 400 years of production. Besides aluminium and paper and pulp holdings, CVRD mines gold, manganese and bauxite.
If pulled off without snags, the CVRD sale should also bury lingering concerns over President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's commitment to transform the Brazilian economy.
Over two years since he was sworn into office, Cardoso has had only shown moderate success in advancing an ambitious legislative reform agenda.
What is more, the total value of assets privatized under the Cardoso administration falls short of those sold off by his predecessor, Itamar Franco.

Analysts say that placing CVRD in private hands would send a powerful signal that Brazil's governing elite has finally become convinced that the country's future growth can only be financed through private investment.

Government planners sighed with relief when the two groups confirmed their interest in CVRD. The government needed at least two competing bidders to demonstrate to the world that the auction would be transparent and to show Brazilians that private investors were eager to buy-up the company.
For all these reasons the Vale sale has generated bitter opposition from just about every sector of Brazilian society.

Over past few weeks unions, congressmen, state employees, landless peasants, prominent artists, two former presidents and all of the country's Roman Catholic bishops have expressed resistance to the company's privatization.

"I oppose the sale (because) the government has not explained why it wants to sell and because hasn't encouraged a debate. Vale turns a profit," said leftist congressman Miro Texeira, a leader of congressional efforts to stop the sale.
The government has still not cleared the legal minefield layed out to stop Tuesday's privatization auction, but is confident the toughest resistance has already been overcome.

Planning Ministry sources say their only real concern is a court case currently in the hands of a Rio de Janeiro judge who has a record of issuing last minute injunctions which have delayed, but never derailed, previous privatization auctions.
